newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sydney bed tax may scare away Japanese tourists.
newsitem.headline: Sydney bed tax may scare away Japanese tourists.

text.p: A proposed bed tax on Sydney hotels could strike a blow against Australian tourism by raising fares on package tours for Japanese travellers, their best customers, travel experts say.

Higher tour prices would also give an edge to other holiday spots, just as Japanese enthusiasm for beaches and resorts down under appears to be fading in favour of more traditional destinations like Hawaii and Europe, they say.

"Sydney is Australia's gateway, and we don't know how much product value a tour without Sydney would have. We would be forced to put more energy into other countries which are less costly than Australia (if the tax takes effect)," Takashi Hiroshima, a spokesman for Japan's second largest travel agency, Kinki Nippon Tourist Co Ltd, said.

The New South Wales state budget announced in early May included a 10 percent accommodation tax on hotels in inner and north Sydney. The tax would help cover the government's A$2.1 billion ($1.58 billion) contribution to projects for the Sydney 2000 Olympics.

"If the tax is adopted it would have to be paid by our customers. This means that we will include the tax in our tour fares, leading to a rise in prices," said Akira Otani, public relations manager at Tokyu Tourist Corp, one of Japan's leading travel agencies.

Yuri Sakamoto, a spokeswoman for Japan Travel Bureau Inc (JTB), Japan's largest travel agency, added: "Australian resorts such as Sydney, the Gold Coast and Cairns became a new option for the Japanese after the waning of the earlier boom of Hawaiian beaches. But that fad is now subsiding as Hawaii, the mainland United States and Europe are regaining momentum."
Japanese tourists often take short-term trips overseas, preferring to travel in organised groups which visit several destinations.
In tours of Australia, Sydney is always included as one of the country's most popular attractions and its airport is the most convenient for connecting flights to and from Japan, Sakamoto said.
The surprise announcement of the bed tax, which is expected to take effect on September 1, spurred concern among Sydney hoteliers that it would restrain tourist visits.

Tourism is Australia's single largest foreign exchange earner and Japan has been the nation's single biggest tourism market since 1990, according to the Australian Tourist Commission, generating more than A$3.6 billion ($2.7 billion) annually.

The boom in Japanese travel to Australia ebbed after 1993, however, with growth slowing to 3.9 percent in 1996 compared to 63.4 percent growth in 1988, according to figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. (A$1 = $0.7510)
